content: Fat choy, also known as Nostoc flagelliforme, is a terrestrial cyanobacterium, a type of photosynthetic bacteria, that is commonly used as a vegetable in Chinese cuisine. When dried, it resembles black hair, which is why its Chinese name translates to hair vegetable. Upon soaking, it develops a very soft texture, similar to fine vermicelli, and its appearance closely resembles long, black human hair. Fat choy naturally grows on the ground in regions such as the Gobi Desert and the Qinghai Plateau. However, over-harvesting in areas like the Mongolian steppes has exacerbated soil erosion and desertification. In response, the Chinese government has imposed restrictions on its harvesting, which has led to an increase in its market price. This scarcity has resulted in some commercially available fat choy being adulterated with strands of non-cellular starchy materials, along with other additives and dyes. Authentic fat choy is dark green in color, whereas counterfeit versions often appear black. In Chinese culture, the last two syllables of the name fat choy in Cantonese sound similar to a phrase meaning struck it rich, although the tonal pronunciation differs. This resemblance is reflected in the popular Cantonese saying Gung hei faat choi (恭喜发财), which translates to Congratulations and be prosperous, a common greeting during Chinese New Year. As a result, fat choy is a favored ingredient in dishes prepared for the Chinese New Year. It is often enjoyed as an alternative to cellophane noodles and is primarily used in Cantonese and Buddhist cuisines. Occasionally, it is also included as an ingredient in hot pot dishes. From a health perspective, research conducted by the biochemistry department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong has highlighted significant concerns regarding fat choy. International studies have shown that fat choy has no nutritional value and contains Beta-methylamino L-alanine (BMAA), a toxic amino acid. BMAA has been found to interfere with the normal functioning of nerve cells. Professor Chan King-ming, a member of the research team, has warned that consuming fat choy could potentially contribute to the development of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and dementia.
